title: GPU runtime debugging and tenant triage checklist
author: Leena Kapoor
body:
Summary

This playbook is a concise, ordered checklist for on-call engineers and infra SREs to triage GPU runtime incidents that impact tenant throughput, tail latency, or availability. It covers quick health checks, tenant isolation checks, CI/IaC failure modes, and safe remediation steps. Use this document when a tenant or pool reports increased errors, slow tokens, or abnormal GPU behavior.

Scope
- Applies to Redwood hosted GPU pools and edge clusters managed by eng-infra.
- Includes multi-tenant and fractional-GPU scenarios, dedicated pools, and spot-backed fallback tiers.
- Does NOT replace the full incident runbook (see related_pages) — this is the operational triage checklist to get from alert to stable.

Ownership
- Primary owner: eng-infra GPU reliability squad.
- Escalation: eng-sre for cross-region network issues, eng-serving-runtime for kernel-level regression, eng-platform for CI/IaC gating regressions.

How to use this doc
1) Run the Preflight checks in order.
2) If root cause is identified, apply the targeted remediation.
3) If issue spans multiple tenants or regions, follow the Incident Response doc and notify Product/Security as required.

Preflight checks (0–5 minutes)
- Confirm the alert: check PagerDuty incident and correlate with Grafana dashboards (gpu-utilization, per-tenant-p99-latency, scheduler-errors).
- Confirm blast radius: identify affected tenants and regions via the request router logs and token-level traces.
- Preserve state: do NOT recycle pods unless instructed; take a heap/profile snapshot for runtime teams.

Quick visibility matrix (what to check first)
- Metrics: GPU utilization, GPU memory pressure, host OOMs, scheduler reject rate, pod restart count, k8s node conditions.
- Logs: kubelet, runtime pod logs, containerd, dmesg, nvidia-smi (on-host), nv-host-engine logs if present.
- IaC/CI: check recent Terraform deploys, pipeline runs, and canary-promote events in the last 30 minutes.

Runtime triage steps (ordered)
1) Node health (cluster-level)
   - kubectl get nodes -o wide | grep NotReady or Kubelet-related taints.
   - Check node memory pressure: kubectl describe node <node> and dmesg /var/log/messages for OOM killers.
   - Run on-host: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=timestamp,name,utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,memory.total,memory.free --format=csv -l 1 (if available).
2) Pod and container checks
   - kubectl get pods -n redwood-serving -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,STATUS:.status.phase,RESTARTS:.status.containerStatuses[*].restartCount --field-selector=status.phase!=Running
   - kubectl logs pod -c runtime --since=15m to spot repeated errors (e.g., KV cache misses, backend timeouts).
3) Scheduler and queueing
   - Inspect router tracing for request queuing and prefix-cache misses.
   - Check batch queue length and worker saturation metrics (auto-batcher backlog).
4) Memory/KV cache consistency
   - Look for sudden increases in KV eviction or cache miss rates. Suggest rolling a cache warm-up if eviction rate is >10% sustained for 5m.
5) Network and egress
   - Confirm node egress connectivity (curl to health-check endpoints across AZs), check VPC flow logs for DENY entries.
   - For cross-account or peered VPCs, validate that the peering route tables have not been modified in the last deploy window.

CI/IaC checks (5–15 minutes)
- Terraform: terraform state list | grep redwood_gpu; check recent runs in the last 2 hours for changes to nodePools, subnet-route tables, or egress firewall rules.
- CI: Inspect the last green canary pipeline for the GPU runtime bundle promotion. If a signed runtime was promoted in the last hour, consider rolling back to previous signed bundle.
- Image artifacts: validate image digest match: docker inspect --format='{{.Id}}' registry.redwood.com/gpu-runtime:<tag> and compare with canary manifest.

Common root causes and targeted remediations
- Cause: Sudden node OOMs or host-level memory pressure.
  Fix: Migrate affected tenants off the node (kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data) and scale up a healthy pool. File infra ticket to investigate host kernel OOM logs.
- Cause: Kernel/runtime regression after canary promotion.
  Fix: Revert runtime image to previous digest via CI rollback and re-run canary tests. Notify eng-serving-runtime and attach trace and profile.
- Cause: Network egress rule change prevents access to S3/kms or shared prefix-caches.
  Fix: Reapply last-known-good terraform plan and run smoke tests; if blocked, open change window with netops.
- Cause: Spot preemption cascade.
  Fix: Trigger burst to pre-warmed reserved capacity pool, enable autoscaler fallback policy for affected tenant(s) and notify billing/CS of potential cost impact.

Safe remediation/rollbacks (ordered)
1) If a single runtime image is implicated: revert image tag in the image promotion pipeline (CI) and let the automated canary rollout handle replacement.
2) If nodes are unhealthy: cordon > drain > replace via autoscaling group or Terraform replace for immutable nodes.
3) If network rules are the problem: revert Terraform change or attach emergency egress rule with minimal scope (IP and port) and document the temporary change for audit.

Runbook commands (copyable)
- Confirm GPU hardware state on node: sudo nvidia-smi -q | egrep -A2 "GPU Current Temp"
- Check container GPU usage: docker stats --no-stream --format "{{.Name}}: {{.CPUPerc}} {{.MemUsage}}" | grep runtime
- List recent terraform runs: aws s3 ls s3://terraform-state-redwood/gpu/ --recursive --human-readable --summarize | tail -n 20
- Drain a node safely: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --grace-period=120 --timeout=10m

Alert thresholds (recommended)
- GPU memory pressure: warning 70% | critical 90%
- per-tenant-p99 latency: warning 300ms | critical 700ms
- scheduler-reject-rate: warning 1% | critical 5%
- pod restart rate: warning 0.2/min | critical 1/min

Post-incident checklist
- Attach traced requests and representative flame graphs to the incident ticket.
- Run a targeted eval against a small prompt suite to validate quality/regression after any runtime rollback.
- Update the IaC changelog and add a remediation note if a Terraform plan caused the incident.
- Run a capacity analysis: were autoscaler thresholds adequate? If not, propose new thresholds.

Playbook notes and escalation
- If the issue cannot be stabilized within 30 minutes and affects >2 regions or >10 tenants, escalate to the on-call engineering manager and open an incident bridge.
- For suspected hardware faults (ECC errors, repeated PCI bus errors), involve metal-ops and schedule node quarantine.

Appendix: quick references and links
- Sample health-queries: Grafana dashboard ids: gpu-overview (d/AbC123/gpu-overview), per-tenant-p99 (d/XyZ987/per-tenant-p99).
- Related pages: preflight-gpu-deployment-validation-and-rollback-playbook, gpu-fleet-scaling-metrics-and-oncall-runbook, signed-gpu-runtime-bundle-and-verifier-guidelines (search internal Confluence).
- Contact list: eng-infra-oncall@redwood.ai, eng-serving-runtime-pagers, eng-sre-pagers.
